body.text: In brief
• Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has led the country since 2018, making him one of Europe’s longest-serving leaders.
• Most polls predict a coalition between the centre-right People's Party and far-right Vox.
Spaniards will vote in a general election on Sunday, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez seeking to fend off conservative and far-right challengers to earn yet another term.
Sánchez’s main rival is conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo, while the far-right’s Santiago Abascal is vying to play kingmaker to Núñez Feijóo and usher in a right-wing coalition.

Scarce, unaffordable housing has been arguably the hottest subject of pre-election debates, following nationwide protests over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home, with Sánchez in favour of rent caps and short-lease bans and his main opponent touting deregulation.
Immigration has been another defining issue, both for Sánchez, one of Europe's loudest advocates of immigration's economic benefits, and for Vox, which wants far tighter controls.
Opposition parties made corruption a central theme after convictions involving members of Sánchez's inner circle and family, though they failed to tie Sánchez to the scandals.
Sánchez has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.
Here's what you need to know about the top candidates.
Pedro Sánchez has led a progressive government since 2018
Sánchez, the secretary-general of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, has led Spain's government since 2018, making him one of Europe's longest-serving leaders.
With his polished appearance and command of English, Sánchez has become a darling of the global progressive movement.
He has staked out strong positions against United States President Donald Trump and the US-Israeli war against Iran, as well as Israel's military operations in Gaza.

He has remained firm on his pro-migration policies amid a wider anti-immigration mood sweeping the developed world. He has overseen Europe's fastest-growing major economy for several years, but greater wealth has not helped extinguish anger over rising housing costs.
Sánchez, 54, is a fierce campaigner who has outwitted adversaries both inside and outside his party and repeatedly beaten the odds, earning him the reputation of a political escape artist.
The most recent example of his electoral savvy came in 2023 when Sánchez’s Socialist Party took a beating in regional elections.
Instead of licking his wounds, the very next day he stunned the country by calling for a general election, and he campaigned on fears of the far right entering government.
The audacious move worked, and voters let him stay in office after forming another left-wing coalition.

Now the trained economist arguably faces his greatest challenge. He is dogged by legal cases involving corruption by a former minister and top officials in his party as well as his wife — who denies wrongdoing.
Sánchez’s fate will most likely depend not only on his Socialists rallying but also on a group of smaller parties to the left outperforming polling that predicts they will lose votes.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo projects himself as a sensible centre-right administrator
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the Popular Party is a lifelong civil servant-turned-politician who has avoided scandal and presents himself as a sensible, moderate, and effective centre-right administrator.
Known nationally by his second-to-last name, Feijóo won election after election in Galicia during the 13 years he governed the rural northwest corner of Spain.
Despite being a less-developed region, Galicia has a long tradition of producing strong politicians.
Among them were 20th-century dictator Francisco Franco and former prime minister Mariano Rajoy, who led Spain from 2011 until 2018 — the last time the Popular Party led the country.
Feijóo, 65, wants to reduce government regulations and lower taxes and, like Sánchez, is staunchly pro-European Union. If he wins, Feijóo is expected to mend bridges with the US and Israel.
Feijóo made the leap to take over his party in time to lead it during the previous general election, when he failed to oust Sánchez.
That means the pressure is on Feijóo to make good on the broad support the Popular Party has maintained since then.

While the low-key Feijóo may be overshadowed by his rivals, he is in charge of the Popular Party's finely tuned vote-winning machine, which is entrenched in the capital, Madrid, as well as many of Spain's rural provinces.
Santiago Abascal and Vox aim for a role in a right-leaning coalition

Bearded and barrel-chested in his tailored suits, Santiago Abascal is a member of the global populist right who exudes macho toughness, and his candidacy could ensure Feijóo has a coalition to govern.
Abascal, 50, is from Spain’s northern Basque Country.
Like many politicians from across the spectrum in Spain, his ultra-nationalist ideology was shaped in response to the violence of the region’s separatist group ETA, which disbanded in 2018.

The first part of Abascal’s political career was as a rank-and-file member of the Popular Party before he and others splintered off to found Vox in late 2013. He quickly took over as its leader and has maintained firm control of the party ever since.
His ideology fits within the wider populist right movement, from the US to Europe.

He is a staunch defender of Israel and has strongly criticised Spain's position under Sánchez toward the country. He wants to slash government regulations for business and cut taxes, and is an open admirer of Argentinian President Javier Milei.
Like Milei, Abascal slams progressive causes, including feminist thought, while dismissing climate change.
Vox is not openly hostile to the EU, unlike other far-right European parties, but Abascal blames immigration for Spain's cost of living pains.
Far-right parties like Vox have been boxed out of government in Spain since the return of democracy following Franco's death in 1975.

After losing seats in the 2023 election, Vox is aiming for a rebound that would afford it the leverage to demand ministries as a junior member in what Abascal hopes will be Feijóo's triumphal government.
Smaller parties might be influential in a close vote
Right-wing voters who find Vox too mild can opt for Se Acabó la Fiesta (The Party Is Over), the political vehicle of a far-right social media influencer.
On the other end of the spectrum, infighting prevented smaller progressive parties from remaking the electoral coalition that helped the left stay in power in 2023.
This time, the Frente Amplio (Broad Front) will compete with Podemos (We Can) for the most left-leaning of voters.
That will hurt both their prospects and Sánchez's shot at forming another left-wing coalition.

There are also traditional parties that focus on influencing how policies and laws impact their home territories. These regionalist parties in Catalonia, the Basque Country, Galicia and the Canary Islands could play a role in forming a ruling coalition if the results are close.
Why is Spain voting now?
Sanchez called the election after parliament, on 2 October, rejected his decrees to address growing anger over rising rents and evictions.

The call was widely seen as an attempt to harness the momentum of housing protests and repair political damage from a migration crisis in Spain's north African enclave of Ceuta, a deadly train crash in January and corruption probes involving his inner circle.
Another train crash occurred on 28 October, and so far Sánchez's plan to mobilise the left appears to be falling short.
Who is ahead in the polls?

Practically all opinion polls point to a potential coalition between the People's Party and far-right Vox as the only combination to win enough votes for an absolute majority in the 350-seat lower house of parliament.
The People's Party is seen as the largest party at around 31 per cent, while Vox stands at roughly 18 per cent, with younger and male voters propelling it, pollsters predict.

Despite a recent modest rise to almost 30 per cent, Sánchez's Socialist Party is mostly expected to come a close second. Parties further to the left, which would be key to a coalition, are polling jointly at around 10 per cent.
